blocks.x: Well, I'm 52 years old, born and I moved to New Orange when I was three. And the first time I remember anything about jazz was at Pastor Shand, this small Negro band called the Watson Brothers. Started off the homemade instruments and they finally, by going around and serenading people in the evening, and people would go out and either pay them because they liked it or pay them to get away. They managed to acquire enough money to buy a few little, I think they had a banjo and a guitar, and I don't remember exactly all the various things that they did have. And they used to play what was, I suppose, jazz. But we loved it and they used to play on the, for dances we used to have on our end of the pier band house. And that was when I was maybe 12 or 13, 14. And then the first Negro band that I saw at playing at New Orleans parties was, when I was around 15 or 16, several people had, uh, dances at home. And they'd have, uh, this Negro band, Celestan, played in that band. And I don't remember whether it was his band or whether it was, he was just a member of it. Was that by 1920? That was around 1920, yeah. And, um, then I didn't see any more, hear any more jazz until we collect records. We had a lot of, you know, those, uh, what was it, Bessie Smith? The blues thing?

The blues thing? That's the thing. Yeah. Well, uh, then we had, uh, old, the Yarns Rhythm Kings, the, uh, the original Dixieland band. And I remember when I went off to school, I took two Puron records up to, uh, School of New York with them. What was that? They thought it was just noise. That was in 1923. They, they didn't appreciate it at all. And I got embarrassed after I played it once or twice and they all thought it was so horrible that I never played it anymore. Then the next year I made my debut and Puron played all of our parties. And he played, uh, popular tunes, you know, the songs of the day, but in a jazz sort of way. And, um, well then we used to go out, I was one of the ones who used to go out to the halfway house. I wasn't allowed in it. It was a sort of a road house and was supposed to be rather shady. So I wasn't allowed to go in the place, but we used to sit out and listen to the music. And they had a wonderful orchestra. Then the, um, over here at the pass, sometimes we'd go to, uh, when the Negroes would have dances, just a bunch of us, you know, teenagers, used to, uh, go and park near the Negro dance hall. And they used to play wonderful music. Just marvelous. And, uh, then I can say when, uh, Pierron was, uh, one of the, uh, he was the most popular jazz band played in our era. But, uh, I know some things that Jack has told me because he was in on this sooner than I was. But there was a band called Robichaux that used to play at the, uh, Louisiana that was very, very popular in 1918. And, uh, then Pierron used to play out at, uh, the, uh, Tranchini's out in Spanish Forth. And, uh, that was a great place for me that they used to go to. But to me, one of the ones that who first took up jazz, uh, was Dr. Souchon, Edmond Souchon. Because he had this old band when he was going to Tulane, the 6th and 7th band. And they used to play jazz. And, uh, he, uh, he knows more about it, I think, probably than almost anyone. From the early jazz that was played, you know, in those days.

Well, do you remember what your parents and your friends' parents thought about it, and what your friends thought about it when it first started, you know, having any work, it first started becoming acceptable? Well... Good Society in New Orleans, have it played a part in David Dorn part in the best life?

It was, Pierron was already established that the country club for us came there, so I don't know, it was before my time that he started playing there. And all of my friends loved it. Their parents didn't care for it too much. But, uh, I remember when I was at Newcomb, uh, that was in 1922, I guess. They, um, uh, there was a Negro, uh, sanitary near Newcomb. And, um, they would, uh, always have a band, you know, going, uh, preceding the funeral procession. And they'd play very slow duages going to the cemetery. And then coming back, they'd really break out and play wonderful jazz. We used to be, you know, sitting out on the campus sometimes, studying, and we'd hear them just really going to town, or going home from the funeral. But, um, as I say, there are several others that know a whole lot more about it, the early start, because it was fairly well established by the time I made my debut.
Well, uh, can you tell me how long it lasted, what, you know, when people stopped listening to it, and then when they started again, they established it?

Well, I think that there were a lot of, uh, these sweet bands that got popular. But, uh, was Puron playing when you, uh, made your debut? But he died, uh, not too long after that. And, uh, then this, let's say, five or six years, or maybe a little bit longer than that, the people started going in for the, you know, the, uh, sweet type of music. Or during the 30s, they, they liked that type. And, uh, I think Puron, I mean, uh, um, South Stan got his dog back here at the pass. Because, you know, John Curran got him to come over here. And, of course, all of our generation just logged it, and the kids picked it up, and then they started having him for, playing in New Orleans again. That's all I know.
Well, that's fine. Thank you, ma'am.

I remember now that, um, the first Negro jazz band that played at, uh, any social white artists in New Orleans was called a Tuxedo Band. And South Stan was not the leader, but he was a member of the band. And that, they played for private parties. And they might have played at the country club, but that was before my time. So I wouldn't know it was, I would say, in, around 19, 18, or 19.
Well, what about this party? How, how old you were? You were born in 1905, right? Mm-hmm. So, how old you were at this party? And, uh, tradition?

Oh, well, he played at the birthday party. I, let's see, it might, I was either 14 or 16, I can't remember. And, uh, it was just a dance at home. And this same Tuxedo Band played at several of the parties, and they also used to play at the, little, um, the fraternity, the high school fraternity party. What was it? About seventh stuff.

segments.title: Watson Brothers band and first Negro band at parties
segments.summary: She recalls the homemade-instrument Watson Brothers serenading and playing for dances, then the first Negro band at home parties around 1920 with Celestin in it.

segments.title: Records, Piron's parties, roadhouses, Robichaux and Dr. Souchon
segments.summary: She took Original Dixieland records to school in New York in 1923 and was embarrassed; Piron played her debut parties; she listened outside the roadhouse and Negro dance halls. She names Piron as most popular band of her era, Robichaux in 1918, Piron at Tranchini's, and Dr. Edmond Souchon as an early jazz pioneer.

segments.title: Parents' attitudes and funeral bands near Newcomb
segments.summary: Friends loved jazz but parents disliked it; she recalls funeral bands playing dirges then jazz near Newcomb in 1922.

segments.title: Sweet bands in the 1930s and Celestin's revival
segments.summary: Piron died, sweet bands took over in the 1930s, and Celestin's return was encouraged, with young people reviving jazz.

segments.title: The Tuxedo Band at private parties
segments.summary: She adds that the Tuxedo Band was the first Negro jazz band at white social events, playing her birthday party and fraternity parties.
